contentMarkdown:
# Agentic AI

Agentic AI describes AI systems that can pursue goals through sequences of actions with some degree of autonomy. In LLM-based applications, this often includes selecting tools, responding to results, and adapting the next step within defined limits.

Usage varies across vendors and products. Some systems follow mostly predefined workflows; others let a model choose more of the process. State which decisions are delegated when describing a system as agentic.

## Example: preparing a trip proposal

A travel assistant receives dates, a budget, and arrival constraints. It retrieves flight options, compares eligible results, and prepares a proposal.

If no option meets the constraints, it can explain the conflict and ask which condition the traveler wants to change. It should preserve the budget unless the user authorizes a change.

The product might allow autonomous research while requiring explicit approval before purchasing. That boundary is part of the system's design.

## Agents, workflows, and multiple agents

An AI agent is a system that takes actions toward a goal. A workflow coordinates steps and dependencies. An agentic product can combine a fixed workflow with model-driven decisions inside particular steps.

Multiple agents are optional. Splitting work among several agents adds coordination requirements and should have a clear purpose.

## Questions for product teams

Identify the decisions the AI may make, the evidence it must use, and the actions requiring authorization. Set limits on duration and resource use.

Evaluate completion against the requested outcome and constraints. Also inspect failed and abandoned runs: a system that completes an easy demonstration may still struggle with missing information, changed conditions, or unavailable tools.

## Related terms

- [Agent Harness](/glossary/agent-harness.html)

- [Autonomous Workflow Orchestration](/glossary/autonomous-workflow-orchestration.html)

name: AI Agent
definition: An AI agent is a system that observes information about its environment and chooses actions toward a goal. In current LLM-based products, an agent often uses a language model to decide which tools to call, inspect the results, and select a next step.
contentMarkdown:
# AI Agent

An AI agent is a system that observes information about its environment and chooses actions toward a goal. In current LLM-based products, an agent often uses a language model to decide which tools to call, inspect the results, and select a next step.

The broader AI concept also includes systems built without language models. An agent's autonomy depends on the decisions and actions its application permits.

## How an LLM-based agent works

A typical interaction includes a goal, available context, a set of permitted tools, and a loop that evaluates tool results before continuing or stopping. Persistent memory and multiple cooperating agents are optional design choices.

ReAct is one research approach that interleaves reasoning and actions. It illustrates how a model can interact with external information while working through a task; it is not a requirement for every agent.

## Example: investigating a delayed order

A support agent receives an order reference, retrieves the order, checks shipment tracking, and summarizes the available evidence. It may ask for clarification if the reference matches more than one order.

The application can allow these read operations while requiring an authorized person to approve a replacement shipment. A tool result should establish whether the replacement was actually created.

## What designers should define

Specify the task boundary, available actions, stopping conditions, and escalation path. Make progress and important outcomes visible to the user.

Test missing data, tool failures, and ambiguous requests. A plausible final message is insufficient evidence of success when the task requires a change in another system.

## Related terms

- [Agentic AI](/glossary/agentic-ai.html)
- [Agent Harness](/glossary/agent-harness.html)
- [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](/glossary/model-context-protocol-mcp.html)
- [Tool Calling (Function Calling)](/glossary/tool-calling-function-calling.html)

## Sources

- [Yao et al.: ReAct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)
- [Anthropic: Building Effective Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents)

name: Agent Harness
definition: An agent harness is the runtime and supporting infrastructure that enables an AI model to operate as an agent. It manages the interaction between model calls, tools, task state, and the execution environment.
sources: Anthropic: Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents (https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)
contentMarkdown:
# Agent Harness

An agent harness is the runtime and supporting infrastructure that enables an AI model to operate as an agent. It manages the interaction between model calls, tools, task state, and the execution environment.

The exact boundary varies by implementation. In Anthropic's Managed Agents architecture, the harness runs the loop that calls the model and routes tool calls, while sessions and sandboxes are separate abstractions.

## What it can include

Depending on the application, a harness may provide:

- Tool definitions, argument checks, and execution.
- Context assembly and state persistence.
- Access controls and approval checkpoints.
- Time limits, budgets, and stopping rules.
- Logs, error handling, and recovery behavior.

Some of these capabilities may live in connected services. A harness needs to coordinate with them rather than assume that a model instruction enforces them.

## Example: a support task across sessions

An agent investigates a customer issue and prepares a proposed account correction. Its harness records completed steps, preserves the relevant identifiers, and pauses before a write operation that needs approval.

If the session is interrupted, the resumed run checks the saved state and current account data. It should determine whether an earlier action completed before attempting it again.

For this task, a useful completion record identifies the requested correction, the verified outcome, and any unresolved issue.

## What to evaluate

Test the complete runtime with expired access, failed tools, and interrupted sessions. Evaluate whether it preserves the user's scope and recovers without repeating consequential actions.

The model's capabilities and the harness's behavior both affect the resulting product experience.

## Related terms

- [Design Harness](/glossary/design-harness.html)
- [AI Agent](/glossary/ai-agent.html)
- [Context Engineering](/glossary/context-engineering.html)
- [Tool Calling (Function Calling)](/glossary/tool-calling-function-calling.html)

- [Model Routing](/glossary/ai-model-routing.html)

## Sources

- [Anthropic: Scaling Managed Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/managed-agents)

name: Design Harness
definition: A design harness is a set of design references, implementation constraints, and validation tools that guides AI-assisted interface development. It helps an agent work with a product's existing components, tokens, patterns, and acceptance criteria.
contentMarkdown:
# Design Harness

A design harness is a set of design references, implementation constraints, and validation tools that guides AI-assisted interface development. It helps an agent work with a product's existing components, tokens, patterns, and acceptance criteria.

The term is emerging and its scope varies. There is no single required file format or toolchain. A team should state what its harness includes and which checks it actually enforces.

## What it can contain

- Component documentation and working usage examples.
- Token names and rules for spacing, typography, and color.
- Interaction, content, and accessibility requirements.
- Representative component states and test data.
- Automated checks and a process for reviewing results.

[Figma Code Connect](/glossary/figma-code-connect.html) can link design components to implementation references. [Storybook](/glossary/storybook.html) can document component states and support interaction, visual, and accessibility tests. These are possible ingredients in a harness.

## Example: building a booking form

A task gives an agent the existing field components, date-selection rules, error messages, and responsive examples. It also specifies how focus should move after validation fails.

The agent implements the form and runs the relevant checks. A reviewer then inspects the submitted-data behavior, keyboard interaction, error recovery, and layout with realistic content.

If a required component does not support the scenario, record the gap and make an explicit implementation decision.

## Keep the checks meaningful

Separate instructions from enforced checks. Documentation can request token use; a configured rule or review process determines whether deviations are caught.

Automated accessibility checks cover only some issues. Include manual evaluation and task testing where needed. Maintain the harness when the underlying design system changes.

## Which rules should an AI agent receive?

Give the agent the actual component names, supported imports and properties, token roles, relevant states, and acceptance criteria. Specify where to retrieve the current references and what to do when a required capability is missing.

For example, a rule can require the agent to check the documented date-field API before using a range property. The review then checks the code against that API and tests the field in the complete task.

An [AI-ready design system](/glossary/ai-ready-design-system.html) supplies maintained context. The harness assembles it for a task, while [design QA](/glossary/design-qa.html) helps inspect the resulting experience.

## Related terms

- [Agent Harness](/glossary/agent-harness.html)
- [Design System](/glossary/design-system.html)
- [Evaluation Harness (AI Evals)](/glossary/evaluation-harness-ai-evals.html)

- [AI-assisted Design](/glossary/ai-assisted-design.html)

## Sources

- [Figma: Code Connect Introduction](https://developers.figma.com/docs/code-connect/)
- [Storybook: Testing UI Components](https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-tests)

name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external capabilities and context through a common client-server interface. MCP servers can expose tools, resources, and prompt templates for compatible applications.
contentMarkdown:
# Model Context Protocol (MCP)

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external capabilities and context through a common client-server interface. MCP servers can expose tools, resources, and prompt templates for compatible applications.

It defines how participants exchange information. The AI application determines how to use that information and which operations to permit.

## Host, client, and server

- The host is the AI application that manages the integration.
- A client is the host-side component communicating with an MCP server.
- A server exposes supported capabilities, such as tools or resources.

Servers can run locally or remotely. Available features depend on the implementation and the capabilities supported by both sides.

## Example: checking a support ticket

A support application connects to an MCP server that exposes ticket-search and ticket-update tools. The AI can request ticket data and use the returned records to prepare a response.

The product might permit search while requiring review before posting a reply. The interface should identify the destination ticket and proposed message. The service must enforce access to that ticket when the operation runs.

Connecting a server does not establish that all of its tools are suitable for every user.

## MCP, tool calling, and skills

Tool calling lets a model request an operation with structured arguments. MCP can make tools available through a shared integration protocol. A skill packages procedural instructions that may tell an agent how to use those capabilities.

For a product integration, specify accessible data, permitted actions, review requirements, and failure behavior. Test disconnected servers, expired authorization, and tool errors as part of the user experience.

## Related terms

- [Tool Calling (Function Calling)](/glossary/tool-calling-function-calling.html)
- [Context Engineering](/glossary/context-engineering.html)
- [Agent Skills (SKILL.md)](/glossary/agent-skills-skill-md.html)
- [AI Agent](/glossary/ai-agent.html)

- [Figma MCP Server](/glossary/figma-mcp-server.html)

## Sources
